name: The US Copyright Office on AI and Copyright: Reports, Guidance and Registration Rules
title: The US Copyright Office on AI and Copyright: Reports, Guidance and Registration Rules
answer: The US Copyright Office's artificial intelligence programme is the primary legal reference for anyone publishing AI-assisted media in the United States. Launched in early 2023, it has produced registration guidance for works containing AI-generated material, a three-part report covering digital replicas and the copyrightability of generative AI outputs, and a notice of inquiry that drew over 10,000 comments. Its pages collect the reports, webinars, listening sessions and review board decisions that define how the Office treats AI-assisted works.

sections.body: This is the US Copyright Office's own collection of pages on copyright and artificial intelligence, published at copyright.gov. It gathers the Office's AI initiative, launched in early 2023 to examine the scope of copyright in AI-generated works and the use of copyrighted materials in AI training, together with its reports, registration guidance, webinars, listening sessions and review board decisions. The pages also cover the Office's economic research, including a February 12, 2025 publication on the economic implications of AI for copyright policy. The material spans a 2020 symposium with WIPO through to a pre-publication version of report Part 3 released on May 9, 2025.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The Office opened its study with a Federal Register notice of inquiry in August 2023, which drew over 10,000 comments by December 2023. Its report has appeared in parts: Part 1, published July 31, 2024, addresses digital replicas; Part 2, published January 29, 2025, addresses the copyrightability of outputs created using generative AI; and a pre-publication version of Part 3 was released on May 9, 2025 in response to congressional inquiries and stakeholder interest, with a final version to follow without substantive changes expected. Registration guidance for works containing AI-generated material was published at 88 Fed. Reg. 16,190 on March 16, 2023, and the Office held a webinar on it on June 28, 2023. Review board decisions listed include SURYAST, Théâtre D'opéra Spatial, Zarya of the Dawn and A Recent Entrance to Paradise. Earlier events covered how the motion picture industry uses AI and its impact on performers, and how existing regimes address machine learning, including licensing, exceptions and sui generis data protection.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The notice of inquiry received over 10,000 comments by December 2023. Part 1 of the report was published July 31, 2024, Part 2 on January 29, 2025, and a pre-publication Part 3 on May 9, 2025. Registration guidance appeared at 88 Fed. Reg. 16,190 (March 16, 2023) and the notice of inquiry at 88 Fed. Reg. 59,942 (August 30, 2023). Review board decisions are dated December 11, 2023 (SURYAST), September 5, 2023 (Théâtre D'opéra Spatial), February 21, 2023 (Zarya of the Dawn) and February 14, 2022 (A Recent Entrance to Paradise). The economic research page states that in 2020 over 38 percent of copyright registrations were granted to women authors, compared with 28 percent in 1978.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For anyone publishing AI-assisted media in the United States, this is the reference point for what can be registered and how. The registration guidance and the review board decisions on specific works show how the Office treats human authorship when generative tools are involved, which directly affects whether a publisher can claim copyright in an AI-assisted article, image or video. The report parts on digital replicas and copyrightability, and the record of how the motion picture industry uses AI and what that means for performers, speak to the practical questions media organisations face when adopting these tools.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Media

sections.body: The pages are a hub and a record rather than a single consolidated document, so the substance sits in linked reports, guidance and event transcripts. Part 3 exists only in pre-publication form, with the final version still to come, and the Office states no substantive changes are expected. The economic research page on AI sits alongside material on women's participation in copyright registration, which is not about AI in media. The pages describe the Office's own initiative and do not cover how other countries' rules would apply to US publishers.
